description:
Outpost 01 was conceptualized and brought to life through a collaborative, cross-functional team effort where every member contributed their core strengths:

Nakeisha: Integrated the NASA API and backend programming.

Aria: Handled core game mechanics and overarching programming.

Santun: Designed the 2D UI and established the overall look and feel of the game.

Francis: Integrated 3D design to visualize the lunar base and astronauts on the moon.
summary:
OUTPOST 01 is a browser-based Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. The player is a NASA engineer running a lunar base at the Moon’s South Pole from a first-person control room. They manage power, oxygen and radiation shielding while watching camera feeds of astronauts on a moonwalk (EVA) and listening to crew radio. Every choice is a trade-off: stronger shielding protects the crew but drains the power needed to run the oxygen pump. If crew health hits zero, the mission fails.

This project addresses the challenge by turning real mission-operations thinking into a simple, hands-on game. Solar flares, coronal mass ejections and geomagnetic storms raise radiation. A warning light turns on when a hazard is happening, so players must read the radiation graph, the CME forecast panel and the astronauts’ comms, and can abort the EVA to shelter the crew. 

This project matters because today’s kids are tomorrow’s explorers. OUTPOST 01 lets them feel what it takes to protect a crew on the Moon, and why shielding, life support and space-weather forecasting matter. It is free in any browser, so any child can try it and be inspired toward space science.
details:
OUTPOST 01 is a lunar base survival game that runs in the browser. The player is a NASA engineer at a base at the Moon’s South Pole, seen from a first-person control room. A big window shows camera feeds of astronauts on a moonwalk (EVA), and wall screens show a radiation graph, a CME forecast and the astronaut’s comms. At the console, the player sets a shielding slider and holds an oxygen button. Oxygen drains constantly, and power recovers very slowly. Shielding must match the radiation level to protect the crew, but it costs more power the higher it goes. Oxygen pumping also needs power, so the player is always balancing the two. Solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and geomagnetic storms spike the radiation. A warning light shows that something is wrong and player has to read the graphs and the astronaut’s voice and face, which show how the crew is doing. The player can also abort the EVA to shelter the crew. If crew health reaches zero, the mission is lost. If the crew survives, the mission is won.

Players learn by doing. They see why a lunar base needs radiation shielding, life support and space-weather forecasting, and they practice making decisions under pressure with limited resources. Our goal is to inspire kids toward space science and engineering, while keeping the game engaging enough that older players enjoy it too.

We built it with React and Vite, in JavaScript, HTML and CSS. It uses NASA’s DONKI space-weather database for the CME forecast. It runs on any device with a modern web browser. The game logic is separate from the interface, and all balance numbers sit in one config file, so the difficulty is easy to tune.

We think our project is creative because the control room is hand-drawn pixel art by our team artist. The slider, oxygen button and camera buttons are frame-by-frame sprite animations, like old-school arcade and horror-game control panels.

We wanted it to be accessible, so there are no accounts, downloads or installs. We kept the look simple and uncluttered for kids, while the trade-offs keep it interesting for older players. We also balanced the difficulty so players always have a fair chance: hazards come with quiet periods in between, the warning light gives advance notice, and the CME forecast shows the impact probability rising before a storm hits.
